q:
Read the passage carefully and answer Q1–Q5:
"Libraries have long served as quiet sanctuaries of collective human memory. Although digital devices now place millions of pages inside a pocket, a physical library still offers something algorithms rarely provide: serendipity—the unexpected discovery of an unfamiliar book sitting beside the one you sought. Moreover, public libraries remain vital democratic spaces where learners of every economic background enjoy equal access to knowledge without commercial barriers."
According to the passage, what unique experience does a physical library provide that algorithms rarely offer?
e: The passage explicitly highlights "serendipity—the unexpected discovery of an unfamiliar book sitting beside the one you sought" as something physical libraries offer over algorithms.

q: Why does the passage (Q1) call public libraries "vital democratic spaces"?
o: Because political debates are held inside them daily
Because they only stock books on constitutional law
Because every citizen must vote to elect the librarian
Because learners of all economic backgrounds get equal access to knowledge without commercial barriers
e: The final sentence explains that public libraries offer "equal access to knowledge without commercial barriers" to learners of every economic background.

q: In the passage (Q1), the word "sanctuaries" most nearly means:
e: "Sanctuary" denotes a quiet, safe refuge or place of protection, fitting "quiet sanctuaries of collective human memory".

q: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage in Q1?
o: The Enduring Value of Public Libraries
e: The passage focuses on why physical public libraries retain unique intellectual and democratic value even in the digital era.

q: Which word in the passage (Q1) is opposite in meaning to "familiar"?
e: "Unfamiliar" (formed with negative prefix "un-") is the direct antonym of "familiar" appearing in the passage.

q: Identify the part of speech of the underlined word: There is "little" milk left in the jug.
e: Here "little" modifies the uncountable noun "milk" (showing quantity), so it functions as an Adjective of Quantity.

q: Fill in the blank with the correct verb: Slow and steady ____ the race.
e: "Slow and steady" expresses a single unified proverbial idea (steady perseverance), so it takes the singular verb "wins".

q: Fill in the blank correctly: Water ____ at 100 degrees Celsius at standard atmospheric pressure.
e: Universal scientific truths and natural laws always use the Present Simple tense ("boils").

q: Choose the correct preposition: The cat jumped ____ the table.
e: "Onto" indicates motion toward a higher surface ("jumped onto the table"), whereas "on" denotes static position.

q: Fill in the blank with the correct article: She is ____ university professor in Lucknow.
e: "University" starts with the consonant sound /juː/ ("yoo"), so it takes the indefinite article "a" (not "an").

q: Identify the correctly spelt word:
e: Following the classic rule "i before e, except after c", the correct spelling is "Receive".

q: Choose the word closest in meaning to "CANDID":
e: "Candid" means truthful, outspoken, and frank (antonym: evasive/deceitful).

q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to "ANCIENT":
e: "Modern" is the direct antonym of "Ancient" ("archaic" and "antique" are synonyms).

q: What does the idiom "once in a blue moon" mean?
e: "Once in a blue moon" means an event that happens extremely rarely.

q: Fill in the blank with the correct verb: The committee ____ divided in their opinions on the new proposal.
e: A collective noun ("committee, jury, team") takes a PLURAL verb ("are") and plural pronoun ("their") when its members act individually or are divided.

q: Choose the correct verb: A pair of spectacles ____ lying on the desk.
e: While "spectacles" alone is plural, the phrase "A pair of + plural noun" takes a SINGULAR verb ("is") agreeing with "pair".

q: Fill in the blank with the appropriate preposition: He was accused ____ stealing confidential documents.
e: "Accused" always takes "of" ("accused of"), whereas "charged" takes "with" ("charged with").

q: Choose the correct preposition: Divide these sweets ____ the five children equally.
e: "Between" is normally used for two entities (or specific pairwise relations), while "among" is used when distributing to more than two individuals collectively.

q: Complete the Type-3 conditional sentence: If she had studied harder, she ____ the scholarship.
e: Type-3 past unreal conditionals follow the strict pattern: "If + Past Perfect (had studied), subject + would have + V3 (would have won)."

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: He said to her, "When will the train arrive?"
o: He asked her when the train would arrive.
He asked her when would the train arrive.
He told her when the train would arrive.
He asked her that when the train would arrive.
e: In Wh-questions, "when" acts as the conjunction (no "that"), "will" backshifts to "would", and subject-verb order becomes assertive ("the train would arrive").

q: Change into Indirect Speech: The teacher said, "Work hard if you want to succeed."
o: The teacher advised the students to work hard if they wanted to succeed.
The teacher ordered that work hard if you wanted to succeed.
The teacher requested to work hard if they want to succeed.
The teacher said that work hard if they wanted to succeed.
e: An advisory imperative converts using "advised [object] + to + V1", and the subordinate verb "want" backshifts to "wanted" with "you" → "they".

q: Change into Passive Voice: Who taught you French?
o: By whom were you taught French?
Who was taught French by you?
By whom you were taught French?
By who were you taught French?
e: "Who" becomes "By whom", followed by Past Simple auxiliary "were" + subject "you" + V3 "taught" + retained object "French".

q: Transform into Superlative Degree: No other river in India is as sacred as the Ganga.
o: The Ganga is the most sacred river in India.
The Ganga is one of the most sacred rivers in India.
The Ganga is more sacred than any river in India.
The Ganga is very sacred in India.
e: "No other + singular noun + as...as" transforms directly into the absolute Superlative "the + superlative + singular noun" ("the most sacred river").

q: Transform into a Compound sentence: Owing to ill health, he could not attend the meeting.
o: Because he was ill, he could not attend the meeting.
He was ill, so he could not attend the meeting.
Being ill, he could not attend the meeting.
As he was ill, he could not attend the meeting.
e: A Compound sentence joins two independent clauses using a coordinating conjunction ("so / therefore"). Options A and D are Complex; C is Simple.

q: Choose the sentence with correct use of the Apostrophe:
o: The children's toys were scattered across the room.
The childrens' toys were scattered across the room.
The childrens toys' were scattered across the room.
The child's' toys were scattered across the room.
e: Irregular plural nouns that do NOT end in "-s" ("children, men, women, people") form the possessive by adding "'s" ("children's").

q: Choose the correctly spelt word:
e: "Millennium" has double "l" and double "n" (Mil-len-ni-um, from Latin mille = thousand + annus = year).

q: A government run by a small group of wealthy or powerful people is called an:
e: "Oligarchy" means rule by a few; "Plutocracy" is rule specifically by the wealthy; "Theocracy" is rule by religious priests; "Anarchy" is absence of government.

q: What does the idiom "to burn the midnight oil" mean?
o: To study or work diligently late into the night
To start a sudden fire in anger
e: "To burn the midnight oil" idiomatically means working or studying hard until late at night.

q: Fill in the blank with the right phrasal verb: I cannot ____ his rude behaviour any longer.
e: "Put up with" means tolerate/endure. ("Put out" = extinguish; "put off" = postpone; "put down" = suppress/criticize.)

q: Choose the synonym of "UBIQUITOUS":
e: "Ubiquitous" means seeming to be present everywhere simultaneously (= omnipresent).

q: Choose the antonym of "FRUGAL":
e: "Frugal" (sparing/economical) is directly opposed to "Extravagant" (wasteful/lavish).

q: Fill in the blank correctly: All ____ glitters is not gold.
e: After indefinite pronouns like "all, everything, nothing, none, only, the same" and superlatives, the relative pronoun "that" is preferred over "which/who".

q: Identify the segment containing a grammatical error: "Scarcely had the minister (A) / finished his speech (B) / than the electricity (C) / went off suddenly. (D)"
e: "Scarcely" and "Hardly" must be paired with "when" (or "before"), NEVER "than" ("than" is paired with "No sooner"). Thus segment C should read "when the electricity".

q: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:
o: Many a brave soldier have laid down his life for the nation.
Many a brave soldier has laid down his life for the nation.
Many a brave soldiers has laid down their lives for the nation.
Many a brave soldier were laying down his life for the nation.
e: "Many a / Many an" is always followed by a SINGULAR countable noun ("soldier"), a SINGULAR verb ("has"), and a SINGULAR pronoun ("his").

q: Fill in the blanks correctly: The two brothers quarrelled ____ each other ____ the ancestral property.
e: One quarrels "with" a person "over" (or "about") a matter/issue.

q: Convert into Indirect Speech: The stranger said to me, "Will you please show me the way to the station?"
o: The stranger asked me if I would please show him the way to the station.
The stranger requested me to show him the way to the station.
The stranger ordered me to show him the way to the station.
The stranger inquired whether I showed him the way to the station.
e: "Will you please...?" is a polite request in interrogative disguise and converts naturally to "requested [object] to + V1".

q: Change into Passive Voice: There is no time to lose.
o: There is no time to be lost.
No time is there to be lost.
There is no time being lost.
Time is not there to be lost.
e: Structures with "There is/are + noun + to + V1" convert cleanly to Passive by changing only the infinitive to "to be + V3": "There is no time to be lost."

q: Which of the following is the correct Simple-sentence equivalent of: "He is so dull that he cannot understand this poem."
o: He is too dull to understand this poem.
He is very dull, so he cannot understand this poem.
Because he is dull, he cannot understand this poem.
Being so dull that he cannot understand this poem.
e: Condensing the Complex "so...that...cannot" into "too + adj + to + V1" yields the single-clause Simple sentence "He is too dull to understand this poem."

q: Identify the correctly spelt word:
e: "Conscientious" (con-sci-en-tious, from "conscience" + "-tious") means diligent and guided by conscience.

q: Which sentence uses the Colon (:) correctly?
o: She bought: apples, oranges, and bananas from the market.
She bought three fruits from the market: apples, oranges, and bananas.
Because: she was tired, she went to sleep early.
The principal said: that classes would resume on Monday.
e: A colon should follow a grammatically complete independent clause introducing a list, explanation, or quotation—never split a verb from its direct object (A) or follow "that" (D).

q: What does the French phrase "Fait accompli" mean?
o: An accomplished fact or irreversible action already completed before others can oppose it
A sudden coup d'état in parliament
e: "Fait accompli" (literally "accomplished deed") refers to an irreversible decision already executed before affected parties can object.

q: Fill in the blanks with the correct pair: The loud thunder did not ____ the brave child, though it had a startling ____ on the birds.
e: "Affect" is primarily a verb meaning "to influence", while "effect" is primarily a noun meaning "result/impact".

q: A person who pretends to have moral standards or beliefs that they do not actually possess is a:
e: A "Hypocrite" feigns virtue or beliefs they do not hold. ("Stoic" endures pain without complaint; "Ascetic" practices strict self-denial; "Cynic" distrusts human sincerity.)

q: Choose the sentence that demonstrates proper grammatical parallelism:
o: She likes reading poetry, to paint landscapes, and gardening.
She likes reading poetry, painting landscapes, and tending her garden.
She likes to read poetry, painting landscapes, and she gardens.
She likes poetry reading, to paint landscapes, and to garden.
e: Parallel structure requires items in a coordinate series to share the same grammatical form—here three gerund phrases ("reading...", "painting...", "tending...").

q: Identify the type of the underlined subordinate clause: "Poor as he is", he never compromises his integrity.
e: Fronted "Adjective + as + Subject + Verb" ("Poor as he is" = "Although he is poor") is a classic literary Adverb Clause of Concession.

q: A long narrative poem celebrating the heroic deeds of a legendary figure in elevated style (such as Homer's "Iliad" or Milton's "Paradise Lost") is called an:
e: An Epic is a grand, dignified narrative poem featuring a heroic protagonist, vast setting, supernatural intervention, invocation to the Muse, and "in medias res" opening.

q: Identify the figure of speech in: "The pen is mightier than the sword."
e: Metonymy substitutes an associated attribute for the thing itself: "pen" stands for writing/ideas, and "sword" stands for military force. (Coined by Edward Bulwer-Lytton in "Richelieu", 1839.)

q: Which figure of speech directly addresses an absent person, an abstract quality, or an inanimate object—as in "O wild West Wind, thou breath of Autumn's being"?
e: Apostrophe is a direct address to the dead, absent, or inanimate/abstract ("O wild West Wind!", "Milton! thou shouldst be living at this hour!").

q: Where was William Shakespeare born in April 1564?
e: William Shakespeare (baptized 26 April 1564, died 23 April 1616) was born in Stratford-upon-Avon, Warwickshire, and married Anne Hathaway in 1582.

q: Which famous line is spoken by Hamlet in Act III, Scene 1 as he contemplates life, suffering, and death?
o: "Cowards die many times before their deaths"
"To be, or not to be: that is the question"
e: "To be, or not to be" is Hamlet's most famous soliloquy. ("Cowards die..." = Julius Caesar; "Out, damned spot!" = Lady Macbeth; "Quality of mercy..." = Portia in The Merchant of Venice.)

q: In how many books was the FINAL revised edition (1674) of John Milton's "Paradise Lost" published?
e: "Paradise Lost" was first published in 10 books in 1667, and reorganized into 12 books in the 1674 second edition (splitting Books VII and X) to match Virgil's "Aeneid".

q: What is the title of John Milton's famous sequel epic (1671, in 4 books) depicting Christ's temptation by Satan in the wilderness?
e: "Paradise Regained" (1671) in four books narrates Christ's spiritual victory over Satan's temptations in the desert.

q: Which celebrated lyric poem by William Wordsworth opens with "I wandered lonely as a cloud / That floats on high o'er vales and hills"?
o: The World Is Too Much with Us
Daffodils (I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud)
e: Composed in 1804 (published 1807), "Daffodils" vividly illustrates Wordsworth's ideal of "emotion recollected in tranquillity" ("inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude").

q: In which scenic region of northern England—celebrated throughout his poetry—did William Wordsworth live for most of his life (at Dove Cottage and Rydal Mount)?
e: Wordsworth, Coleridge, and Southey were collectively nicknamed the "Lake Poets" due to their deep association with the Lake District (Cumbria).

q: John Keats died of tuberculosis in February 1821 at the young age of 25 in which European city?
e: Keats died in Rome on 23 February 1821 and was buried in the Protestant Cemetery with his self-chosen epitaph: "Here lies One Whose Name was writ in Water."

q: Which literary movement / dramatic genre is John Galsworthy chiefly associated with as a playwright in early 20th-century England?
o: Realistic Social Problem Play (Drama of Ideas)
e: Influenced by Henrik Ibsen, Galsworthy mastered the realistic Social Problem Play ("The Silver Box", "Strife", "Justice", "Loyalties"), examining class, law, and industrial conflict with cool objectivity.

q: In George Orwell's "Nineteen Eighty-Four", what is the omnipresent slogan displayed on posters across Oceania symbolizing total state surveillance?
e: "BIG BROTHER IS WATCHING YOU" symbolizes the totalitarian surveillance state of Oceania led by the Party. ("All animals are equal..." is from "Animal Farm".)

q: In George Orwell's "Animal Farm", which commandment is eventually altered on the barn wall to justify the pigs' tyrannical privileges?
o: "No animal shall sleep in a bed without sheets"
"All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others"
"Whatever goes upon two legs is a friend"
e: The original Seven Commandments are condensed into one chillingly ironic single maxim: "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others."

q: A poem in which a single fictional speaker addresses a silent listener at a critical moment, inadvertently revealing their own character (perfected by Robert Browning in "My Last Duchess"), is called a:
e: A Dramatic Monologue features (1) a single speaker distinct from the poet, (2) a silent auditor whose presence is implied, and (3) psychological self-revelation.

q: What is "Poetic Licence" in literary criticism?
o: A royal patent granted to the Poet Laureate
A rhyme scheme using only monosyllabic words
The liberty a poet takes to depart from strict rules of grammar, fact, or word order for artistic effect
Copyright permission to publish an anthology
e: Poetic licence allows poets deliberate deviations in syntax, diction, or historical detail to serve metre, rhyme, or imaginative power.

q: Identify the figure of speech in: "The child is father of the man" (Wordsworth, "My Heart Leaps Up").
e: A Paradox (or Epigram) makes an apparently self-contradictory statement that reveals a deeper psychological truth—that childhood experiences shape the adult personality.

q: What is "Pathetic Fallacy" (a term coined by John Ruskin in "Modern Painters", 1856)?
o: Attributing human emotions and sympathies to inanimate nature (e.g., "cruel crawling foam", "weeping skies")
A logical error in an orator's speech
Using mild words to soften harsh realities
e: Ruskin coined "Pathetic Fallacy" for projecting human feelings onto nature. (Mild words for harsh realities = Euphemism.)

q: In Shakespeare's "King Lear", which of Lear's three daughters refuses to flatter him with empty hyperbole, saying she loves him "according to my bond; no more nor less"?
e: Cordelia's honest restraint angers King Lear into disinheriting her, setting the tragedy in motion while deceitful Goneril and Regan betray him.

q: In "The Merchant of Venice", who disguises herself as the young doctor of law "Balthazar" to rescue Antonio from Shylock's bond of a pound of flesh?
e: Portia (heiress of Belmont, aided by Nerissa as her clerk) delivers the celebrated "Quality of Mercy" speech and defeats Shylock on the legal technicality that his bond grants flesh but "no jot of blood".

q: Which of Shakespeare's Roman tragedies features Mark Antony's masterly ironical funeral oration beginning "Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears"?
e: In "Julius Caesar" (Act III, Scene 2), Antony uses repeated verbal irony ("Brutus is an honourable man") to turn the Roman mob against the conspirators.

q: Milton's twin companion poems "L'Allegro" (The Cheerful Man) and "Il Penseroso" (The Thoughtful/Melancholic Man) were composed during which period of his life?
e: During his scholarly retirement at his father's estate in Horton (Buckinghamshire), Milton wrote his finest early lyrics: "L'Allegro", "Il Penseroso", the masque "Comus" (1634), and "Lycidas" (1637).

q: In Book I of "Paradise Lost", what is the stated grand purpose of Milton's epic?
o: To celebrate the martial glory of King Arthur
To mourn the fall of the English Commonwealth
"To justify the ways of God to men"
To recount the voyages of Odysseus
e: Invoking the Heavenly Muse in Book I (line 26), Milton announces his aim to "assert Eternal Providence, / And justify the ways of God to men."

q: In "Ode: Intimations of Immortality from Recollections of Early Childhood" (1807), what philosophical belief regarding the human soul before birth does Wordsworth poetically explore?
o: Platonic pre-existence of the soul ("trailing clouds of glory do we come / From God, who is our home")
e: Drawing on Plato's doctrine of Anamnesis (recollection), Wordsworth portrays childhood as retaining visionary radiance from heaven, which gradually "fades into the light of common day".

q: Which famous sonnet by William Wordsworth laments modern materialism ("Getting and spending, we lay waste our powers") and wishes to be "a Pagan suckled in a creed outworn"?
o: The World Is Too Much with Us
e: "The World Is Too Much with Us" (1807) critiques industrial alienation from Nature, longing to catch sight of Proteus or hear Triton blow his wreathed horn.

q: Which of John Keats's Great Odes celebrates the serene beauty of ripeness and seasonal fulfilment WITHOUT any personal despair, opening with "Season of mists and mellow fruitfulness"?
e: Composed in September 1819 at Winchester, "To Autumn" is universally praised as Keats's most objectively perfect and serene ode, structured across three 11-line stanzas (ripeness, harvest, evening music).

q: In "Ode to a Nightingale", why does Keats declare he is "half in love with easeful Death"?
o: Because dying at the peak of ecstatic communion with the bird's immortal song seems rich and painless
Because he wishes to flee poverty in London
Because he is mourning the loss of his brother George
Because he rejects all beauty in the physical world
e: In Stanza 6, intoxicated by the nightingale's timeless music ("Now more than ever seems it rich to die, / To cease upon the midnight with no pain"), Keats momentarily longs for a peaceful escape from human transience before the word "forlorn" tolls him back to his sole self.

q: Who is the possessive, materialistic central protagonist of "The Man of Property" (1906, the opening novel of "The Forsyte Saga") whose obsession with owning his wife Irene drives the tragedy?
e: Solicitor Soames Forsyte embodies the Victorian "sense of property", treating his unhappy wife Irene as a prized possession, sparking her tragic affair with architect Philip Bosinney.

q: Which 1920 play by John Galsworthy depicts a bitter class-and-property feud between the aristocratic Hillcrist family and the newly rich industrialist Hornblower?
e: "The Skin Game" (1920, later adapted into a film by Alfred Hitchcock) shows how class warfare strips away gentility from both old aristocracy (Hillcrist) and ruthless nouveau riche (Hornblower).

q: In "Animal Farm", which hardworking, loyal cart-horse embodies the exploited, trusting working class with his two mottos "I will work harder" and "Napoleon is always right"?
e: Boxer works tirelessly to build the windmill until he collapses, only to be heartlessly sold by Napoleon to the knacker's yard (horse slaughterer) in exchange for whisky.

q: Which of the following is a 1931 autobiographical essay by George Orwell recounting the execution of a Hindu prisoner in Burma, vividly illustrating "the unspeakable wrongness of cutting a life short"?
e: In "A Hanging" (1931), Orwell observes the condemned prisoner stepping aside to avoid a puddle on his way to the gallows—an unforgettable epiphany of his shared humanity.

q: What is "Blank Verse", as distinguished from "Free Verse"?
o: Blank verse has regular metre (unrhymed iambic pentameter), whereas free verse has neither regular metre nor regular rhyme
Blank verse rhymes in couplets, whereas free verse uses quatrains
Blank verse is used only in sonnets, whereas free verse is used only in epics
Both terms are exact synonyms for unrhymed poetry
e: Blank verse (introduced into English by the Earl of Surrey in his translation of Virgil's Aeneid) maintains strict iambic pentameter without end-rhyme; free verse (vers libre, e.g., Walt Whitman) abandons both regular metre and rhyme.

q: Who coined the term "The Four Great Tragedies" (Hamlet, Othello, King Lear, Macbeth) and analysed Shakespeare's tragic heroes through character psychology in his landmark 1904 book "Shakespearean Tragedy"?
e: Andrew Cecil Bradley's "Shakespearean Tragedy" (1904) shaped 20th-century Shakespeare criticism. (L. C. Knights famously challenged Bradley's character-centred approach in "How Many Children Had Lady Macbeth?", 1933.)

q: In which of Shakespeare's plays does the witty heroine Rosalind disguise herself as the youth "Ganymede" in the Forest of Arden?
e: Rosalind disguises herself as Ganymede in "As You Like It" (whereas Viola disguises herself as Cesario in "Twelfth Night").

q: In "Paradise Lost", which high-ranking fallen angel (Book II) argues in the Pandemonium debate for peaceful sloth and "ignoble ease" rather than renewed war against Heaven?
e: In Book II's infernal council: Moloch argues for open war; Belial argues for passive ease; Mammon proposes building a glittering kingdom in Hell; Beelzebub (voicing Satan's plan) proposes corrupting the newly created Earth and Man. (Abdiel is the lone loyal seraph who rejects Satan in Book V.)

q: In "Lycidas", when St. Peter ("The Pilot of the Galilean lake") denounces the corrupt clergy of the Anglican Church as "Blind mouths!", what literary figure of speech is vividly compressed in "Blind mouths"?
e: John Ruskin famously praised "Blind mouths" (line 119 of "Lycidas") as a masterly compressed Catachresis/Mixed Metaphor: bishops ("overseers") who cannot see ("blind") and pastors ("feeders") who only devour ("mouths").

q: Which Victorian poet and critic famously wrote of Wordsworth in "The Lost Leader" (1845)—"Just for a handful of silver he left us, / Just for a riband to stick in his coat"—criticizing Wordsworth's later political conservatism and acceptance of the Poet Laureateship?
e: Robert Browning wrote "The Lost Leader" (1845) lamenting Wordsworth's abandonment of his youthful French Revolution radicalism.

q: Wordsworth's "Michael" (1800) is subtitled "A Pastoral Poem" and tells the heartbreaking story of an aged Lakeland shepherd and his son Luke building an unfinished:
e: Michael and Luke lay the cornerstone of a sheepfold ("The Evening Star") as a covenant before Luke leaves for the city, where Luke falls into ruin—leaving Michael sitting beside the unfinished sheepfold ("And never lifted up a single stone").

q: Which unfinished epic poem by John Keats (1818–19, deeply influenced by Miltonic blank verse) narrates the fall of the ancient Titans (Saturn and the Sun-god) and the rise of the new Olympian god Apollo?
e: Keats abandoned "Hyperion" (and its revision "The Fall of Hyperion: A Dream") partly because he felt its style had "too many Miltonic inversions".

q: In "On First Looking into Chapman's Homer" (1816)—Keats's breakthrough Petrarchan sonnet—which Spanish explorer does Keats historically confuse with Vasco Núñez de Balboa as "stout ____" staring at the Pacific from a peak in Darien?
e: Keats wrote "Or like stout Cortez when with eagle eyes / He star'd at the Pacific"—a famous historical slip for Balboa, yet immortalized for its breathtaking sense of poetic discovery.

q: Under what pseudonym did John Galsworthy publish his first four early works of fiction ("From the Four Winds", "Jocelyn", "Villa Rubein", and "A Man of Devon") between 1897 and 1901?
e: Galsworthy published under the pen name "John Sinjohn" until his father's death in 1904, after which he published "The Island Pharisees" (1904) and "The Man of Property" (1906) under his own name.

q: In John Galsworthy's play "Escape" (1926), an escaped convict named Matt Denant (imprisoned for accidental manslaughter while defending a woman in Hyde Park) flees across Dartmoor, ultimately surrendering himself in a village church to avoid forcing whom to tell a lie?
e: Denant refuses to let the gentle village Parson compromise his conscience by lying to the pursuing warders, surrendering with the memorable line: "It's one's decent self one can't escape."

q: In "Nineteen Eighty-Four", what is the grim irony of the four Ministries of Oceania (Truth, Peace, Love, and Plenty)?
o: Each Ministry's name is the exact opposite of its actual function (Truth = propaganda, Peace = war, Love = torture, Plenty = rationing)
All four Ministries are run secretly by Eurasia
None of the four Ministries actually exist in London
All four Ministries are headed by Winston Smith
e: Orwell's stark satire of totalitarian Doublespeak names the war ministry "Ministry of Peace", torture/secret police "Ministry of Love", propaganda/lies "Ministry of Truth", and economic scarcity "Ministry of Plenty".

q: In his 1946 essay "Why I Write", George Orwell enumerates FOUR great motives for writing prose: Sheer Egoism, Aesthetic Enthusiasm, Historical Impulse, and which fourth motive that he admits dominates his own mature work?
e: Orwell defines "Political Purpose" in the broadest sense—"desire to push the world in a certain direction"—declaring that since the Spanish Civil War (1936), every serious line he wrote was "against totalitarianism and for democratic socialism".

q: What is a "Zeugma" (as in Alexander Pope's famous line from "The Rape of the Lock": "Or stain her honour, or her new brocade")?
o: Yoking two different nouns (one abstract, one concrete) to a single verb that applies to each in a different sense
Repeating the same word at the beginning of successive clauses
Placing a scene or object in the wrong historical period
Substituting a part of something to represent the whole
e: Zeugma links two words to one governing verb/adjective in distinct (literal + figurative) senses ("stain her honour" = morally, "stain her brocade" = physically). (B = Anaphora; C = Anachronism; D = Synecdoche.)

q: Who coined the critical term "Dissociation of Sensibility" (in his 1921 essay "The Metaphysical Poets") to describe the 17th-century split between thought and feeling that he blamed partly on John Milton and John Dryden?
e: T. S. Eliot argued that John Donne and the Metaphysical poets possessed a unified sensibility ("felt their thought as immediately as the odour of a rose"), whereas a "dissociation of sensibility" set in after the 17th century.
